Reinforcement Learning: Core Concepts and Q-Learning
Building systems that learn optimal decision-making by interacting with an environment and receiving reward signals, without explicit instruction.
— the agent-environment model and the core components that make RL distinct from supervised/unsupervised learning
— how to represent the "goodness" of states and actions, and the algorithm that learns those values
— the Bellman equation, temporal difference error, and how to iteratively refine Q-values through episodes
— why one attempt is not enough and how repeated experience stabilizes learning

Q-Learning turns a sequence of observed rewards into a mental model (Q-table) that the agent can use to make optimal decisions in any state, and that model improves with every episode as long as the agent explores enough to discover all paths.
The Three Branches of Machine Learning
Learning what to do (which action to take) based on rewards and punishments received from the environment.
Map input → output (student with answer key)
Actions → maximize reward (pet learning tricks for treats)

RL differs fundamentally because there is no teacher providing the correct answer. The agent only receives feedback on how good or bad an action was, and must learn which actions lead to high rewards through trial and experience.
The five elements that define every reinforcement learning problem.
The world the agent interacts with (e.g., the grid)
What the agent can do (e.g., move up/down/left/right)
Where the agent is at any moment (e.g., a specific cell in the grid)
Feedback signal from the environment (+ good, − bad, 0 neutral)
The agent receives only feedback signals (rewards/penalties), not instructions or a map, and must gradually learn which actions lead to better outcomes through accumulation.
Agent takes actions and receives feedback (warmer/colder → small ±reward; candy/lemon → large ±reward)
No correct path is given; agent improves by accumulating experience over time
This separation of learning from instruction is what makes RL powerful: it works in environments where the "right" answer depends on context, opponent behavior, or unknown dynamics

Like a pet learning tricks for treats: there is no manual showing the pet the correct behavior. The pet tries actions, receives rewards or not, and gradually learns which actions reliably produce the treat.
Domains where no fixed "correct" answer exists, opponent behavior is adaptive, or the environment is unknown or changing.
No "correct" steering label for every situation
Opponent adapts, no fixed answer key
User feedback is sequential, not one-shot

Should I do what I already know works (exploit), or try something new that might be better (explore)? RL agents must balance greedy choices (highest known Q-value) with random exploration (discovering better paths).
A function that estimates how good a state or state-action pair is, by predicting the total reward an agent will receive from that point onward.
How good it is to be in a given state s (the expected future reward from that state)
How good it is to take a specific action a in a given state s (the expected future reward after taking that action)
method: it learns a value function that, when maximized over actions, determines the optimal policy.
A lookup table storing Q(s,a) for every state-action pair, where each entry represents the estimated long-term value of taking that action in that state.
Cell contents = Q(s,a), the value estimate for that pair

At the start of learning, Q-values are initialized arbitrarily (often to 0 or random numbers). The algorithm corrects them over time. Even if the initial guess is wrong, the learning process converges toward the true values as the agent gains experience.
The observed Q-value is the immediate reward plus the discounted maximum future Q-value available from the next state.
The computed Q-value after this experience
The immediate reward received upon arriving in the next state s'
Discount factor; how much the agent values future rewards relative to immediate rewards
The best Q-value available from the next state (across all possible actions)

The Bellman equation decomposes value into two parts: what you get right now (immediate reward) plus what you can get next (future value, discounted). This recursive structure is why Q-Learning learns efficiently: each update leverages what the agent already knows about future states.
A number between 0 and 1 that controls how much the agent cares about future rewards compared to immediate rewards.
Robot only cares about immediate reward. The future does not matter; only the next step counts.
Future rewards matter half as much as immediate rewards.
Future rewards matter significantly, but slightly less than today's rewards.
Robot values future rewards equally to immediate rewards (all time steps equally important).

A higher γ makes the agent more tolerant of short-term negative rewards when future rewards are promising. This is crucial in environments where the path to the goal incurs temporary costs (like moving through a low-reward zone to reach a high-reward target).
The difference between the observed Q-value (what the agent just learned from experience) and the expected Q-value (what the agent previously thought).
The Q-value computed from the Bellman equation after one action and reward
The Q-value stored in the table before this experience

TDE measures how "surprised" the agent was by this experience. A large positive TDE means the path was better than expected; a large negative TDE means it was worse. This error signal drives learning.
Adjust the stored Q-value toward the observed Q-value, scaled by the learning rate.
Learning rate; how much to adjust the Q-value at each time step (typically 0 < α ≤ 1)
Conservative updates; changes are gradual, reducing noise but learning is slower
Aggressive updates; the new observation heavily overrides the old value, but may oscillate

The update rule is not a replacement—it is a weighted blend of the old Q-value and the new observation. This averaging across experiences is why Q-values eventually stabilize rather than jumping erratically.
Agent is in state S1 with Q(S1, down) = 0.75 in the table
Agent arrives in state S4 and receives reward R(S4) = −1
The observed value is worse than expected (the agent encountered a negative reward).
The Q-table entry is updated from 0.75 to 0.59.
Agent is in state S4 with Q(S4, right) = 0.75 in the table
Agent arrives in state S5 and receives reward R(S5) = −2
Effect of Higher Discount Factor γ
Starting from the same step as S4 → S5 but with γ = 0.9 instead of γ = 0.1:

With γ = 0.1, the Q-value dropped to 0.49. With γ = 0.9, it dropped only to 0.655. The higher discount factor made the agent weight the future reward (2.0 at S5) much more heavily, offsetting the negative immediate reward (−2). This makes the agent more patient about temporary setbacks.
One complete run from start to goal (or failure), during which the agent takes actions and receives rewards until a terminal state is reached.
Agent begins at a starting state (e.g., S1, or randomly chosen)
Agent reaches a goal state (e.g., S9 with +10 reward) or a failure state (e.g., S8 with −10 penalty)
S1 → down → S4 → right → S5 → right → S6 → ... (episode continues until goal or failure)

An episode is bounded. In a real task, "bounded" means the agent either reaches the goal or uses up its allotted steps. This is important: without an end condition, the agent would accumulate infinite rewards and learning would never stabilize.
Why One Episode Is Not Enough
After one episode, Q-values are unstable and inaccurate because the agent has not yet discovered all paths or experienced the full range of rewards.
The agent has only seen one path through the environment
It has not yet discovered the optimal route to the goal
It has not experienced high-reward outcomes (like +10)
Q-values reflect only the partial rewards seen so far (e.g., small negative rewards like −1, −2, −1)
These Q-values do not represent the true value of each state because they are missing critical information about what lies beyond

Q-values do not converge to optimal values after one episode. Multiple episodes with exploration are required because each episode provides only a partial sample of the environment's reward structure.
Each episode gives the agent more experience, allowing it to discover better paths, update Q-values closer to the truth, and eventually converge on an optimal policy.
Different episodes may take different random actions, exploring new paths that lead to higher-reward states
When the agent reaches S5 in a later episode, its Q(S5, a) values are now more accurate (from previous episodes), so the Bellman update at earlier states backpropagates better value estimates
When Q-values stop changing much between episodes, the agent has learned the environment's reward structure and the policy has stabilized
Once Q-values have converged, the agent can extract the optimal policy by always choosing the action with the highest Q-value in each state

Audit (run episode) → Update (refine Q-values) → Explore (try new actions) → Repeat. Each cycle brings Q-values closer to the true value, which represents the discounted future reward from each state-action pair.
Bias in Machine Learning: Sources, Detection, and Mitigation
Understanding how human biases enter ML systems, how they cause unfair outcomes across groups, how to measure and detect bias, and what interventions work.
— the business, quality, and ethical imperatives for building fair systems
— where bias enters the pipeline (historical, representation, measurement, aggregation) and how to recognize each
— Amazon hiring (historical), Optum healthcare (measurement), Gender Shades facial recognition (representation), COMPAS recidivism (fairness metrics in conflict)
— a practical framework: audit data, choose fairness metrics, measure performance by group, apply interventions (pre/in/post-processing), and monitor after deployment

Bias is not a property of the algorithm alone—it is a property of the entire pipeline (data, labels, model, deployment, feedback). Every model must be audited across groups, and no single fairness metric can satisfy all stakeholders; the choice of metric embeds a value judgment about whose errors to prioritize.
ML models are trained on human-generated data, which encodes human decisions and human biases. Models do not correct or erase these biases; they amplify, automate, and legitimize them.
Past human decisions → Training data (encoded with bias)
Model learns patterns from that data → Learns to replicate and generalize bias
Model deployed → Biased decisions applied at scale, automatically, and with the appearance of objectivity

The appearance of mathematical objectivity makes algorithmic bias more dangerous than human bias. A human hiring manager might catch themselves and correct a prejudiced decision. An algorithm looks like math and is trusted without question.
Biased ML systems have caused measurable harm to real people across employment, healthcare, and criminal justice.
Resume screeners filter out candidates based on gender or race, blocking opportunities
Algorithms undertreating minority patients because they use proxy measures that reflect access barriers, not true health need
Risk assessment tools overpredict recidivism for certain demographic groups, leading to harsher sentences and parole denials
— bias = poor generalization to new groups; (3)
— you have power; power creates responsibility.
Systematic, unfair discrimination in model outputs that creates different outcomes for different groups, where group membership should not matter.
Different groups receive the same predictions
No legitimate reason for the difference
Difference reflects a real, relevant property (e.g., different disease prevalence)
The difference hurts members of the disadvantaged group
The difference treats all groups fairly

Bias = difference + unjustified + harmful. If a medical model predicts higher disease risk in a group that genuinely has higher prevalence (due to genetic or environmental factors), that is not bias—it is accuracy. Bias is when the difference reflects data quality, missing information, or historical injustice, not underlying reality.
Past social inequalities are reflected in training data, and the model learns to replicate them.
The world is unfair. Data remembers that unfairness. The model learns from the data.

A loan model trained on past lending approvals learns that certain zip codes (historically redlined by discriminatory policy) have higher default rates. Even if current residents are equally creditworthy, the model downgrades them because the historical data shows a pattern.

Historical bias is the hardest to fix because the bias is in the ground truth itself—the labels in the training data encode real-world discrimination. The model is not doing anything "wrong"; it is learning from biased history.
Training data does not reflect the real-world population; missing voices create blind spots.
If you train only on data from one group, the model learns that group well and performs poorly on all others.

A medical image AI trained mostly on fair-skinned patients performs poorly on darker skin tones. The algorithm never saw many examples of darker skin, so it has not learned the visual patterns that distinguish healthy skin from diseased skin in that population.
Representation bias is the most straightforward to identify: look at the demographics of your training data. If a group is underrepresented, the model will likely underperform on that group.
Features or labels are systematically different across groups, so the model learns the wrong thing.
Using the wrong variable as a proxy for what you actually want to measure.

Using past healthcare costs as a proxy for "health need." But lower-income or underserved groups have lower recorded costs not because they are healthier, but because they have less access to healthcare. The model learns: low costs = low need, and systematically excludes the sickest patients in those groups from extra care.

Similar to using zip code as a proxy for creditworthiness. Zip code is correlated with wealth and credit access due to historical segregation, but it does not measure a person's actual ability to repay. The model conflates geography with financial merit.
A single model forced onto groups with different base rates fails for both.
One-size-fits-all does not work when the underlying populations have different characteristics.

A single recidivism model for two neighborhoods with different crime rates and policing intensity. The model may appear "accurate" when averaged across both neighborhoods but is systematically wrong in each one individually because it cannot account for neighborhood-specific factors.

The fix for aggregation bias is often to build separate models for different groups or to include group-specific features. However, this must be done carefully: disaggregating can reduce data per group and increase variance, or it can be justified as accommodating real differences.
Is past unfairness in my training data?
Does my data look like the real world?
Are my labels valid across groups?
Should I split into multiple models?
Amazon needed to screen millions of resumes for thousands of hires per year. Manual screening was slow and inconsistent.
Amazon's intuition: If ML can recommend products, why can't it recommend resumes?
The plan: Train on past resumes and hiring decisions, let the algorithm learn which resumes led to hires, then rank new resumes automatically
The model learned from old resumes submitted by people already hired. Most of those people were men. The model learned to prefer men.
Past hiring decisions reflected a male-dominated tech industry
Penalize the word "women," downgrade graduates from all-women's colleges, assign lower scores to female-sounding activities
"Most successful past hires were men" → "Resumes like those (male) → higher probability of hire" → "I should rank resumes of men higher"
A woman applying to Amazon would have her resume downranked not because of anything she wrote, but because of patterns in the male-dominated hiring history

The model learned a correlation (male ≈ hired) but inverted causality (hiring is not male because males are better; males were hired because of historical discrimination). The model repeated that mistake.
What Happened After: The Fix Attempts
Bias discovered (2015) → tool discontinued (2017), but attempts to fix failed in between.
Engineers tried to remove gender-related words from the model, adjusted thresholds, ran new tests. But the bias kept coming back through hidden correlations.
If you remove the word "women," the model might learn to penalize typical women's colleges or female-coded activities by name
If you remove those, it might learn to penalize gap years (more common in female resumes in some fields)
The underlying problem—that the training data contains a male-dominated history—cannot be patched by removing features. You must fix the data.

case. The model learned from data that encoded past discrimination. Removing features is post-hoc and fragile. The real solution would have been to reweight training data to balance gender, or audit and correct the hiring decisions in the historical data itself.
Optum built an algorithm to identify "high-risk" patients who need extra care (nurses, check-ins, follow-ups).
Predict future healthcare costs → higher predicted cost = "high risk" → send extra resources
Using past healthcare costs as a proxy for "how sick is this patient?" breaks down when groups have different access to care.
Recorded costs ≈ actual health need. Someone with a chronic illness gets diagnosed and treated, costs are recorded accurately.
Recorded costs << actual health need. Someone with the same chronic illness might not have regular access to doctors, so only emergencies are recorded. Costs look low even though the need is high.
The algorithm systematically excluded the sickest patients in the lowest-access group. At the same level of illness severity, Black patients were half as likely to be flagged for extra care.
Investigation began (2017) → published in Science (2019) → Optum modified algorithm (2019).
Number of chronic conditions + adjustment for access barriers
"Number of chronic conditions" is more directly a measure of health need and is less mediated by access to the healthcare system
case. The label (past costs) did not validly measure the target (health need) across groups. The fix was to choose a better label, not to remove groups or adjust thresholds.
Case Study: Gender Shades Facial Recognition

Joy Buolamwini, an MIT grad student, was working on a facial recognition project for a class. The software worked perfectly on her light-skinned classmates and even recognized a white beauty mask she held up. When she looked at the camera: no detection.
The model was literally blind to her face. This motivated a research question: Is this algorithm trained only on light-skinned faces?
Facial recognition algorithms trained on datasets that are mostly light-skinned faces will perform well on that group and poorly on darker-skinned faces.
What Joy and her team did:
Analyzed existing facial recognition datasets (IJB-A, Adience)
Found representation bias: 80-86% light-skinned faces, only 14-20% darker-skinned faces
Created a balanced test dataset: 1,270 faces, equal representation from 3 African countries + 3 European countries, balanced by gender and skin type
Tested 3 commercial systems: IBM, Microsoft, Face++
Error rates were highest for darker-skinned females—a phenomenon called intersectionality (multiple marginalized categories compound).
Microsoft: Over 93% of misgendered faces were darker-skinned subjects
Face++: Over 95% of misgendered faces were female
IBM: Largest gap (34.4% difference between best and worst groups)

Bias does not affect demographic groups independently. A woman of color can face compounded bias (both gender and race). Gender Shades showed that the three systems failed darkest on the intersection of female + darker-skinned, not just on skin tone or gender alone.
The Gender Shades study changed how companies audit facial recognition systems.
IBM responded in one day, announced changes to Watson Visual Recognition. Microsoft and Face++ began audits and retraining.
Microsoft: 19.28% error reduction for darker females

Improvements were significant but error rates remained higher for darker-skinned subjects. This shows both that the problem is fixable (data + retraining helps) and persistent (structural bias in datasets and development practices is slow to change).
case. Training data was 80-86% light-skinned faces. The model was never exposed to enough darker-skinned examples to learn those patterns well. The fix: collect more diverse data and retrain.
An algorithm used in over 1 million cases across US courts to predict whether a defendant will re-offend within 2 years.
Judges receive a risk score (1-10) for each defendant; scores influence bail amounts, sentencing, and parole decisions
Recidivism (whether someone will be re-arrested within 2 years)
Is COMPAS fair? Do risk scores mean the same thing across racial groups?
Obtained COMPAS scores for 7,000+ defendants in Broward County, Florida (2013-2014)
Tracked whether they actually re-offended within 2 years
Compared model performance across white and Black defendants
COMPAS showed different error patterns across groups.
The Fairness Conflict: Two Metrics, Two Narratives
ProPublica and Northpointe both measured fairness, got opposite conclusions, and were both technically correct.
56% 46% % labeled "high risk" 52% 35% % who actually re- offended
56% 46% % labeled "high risk" 52% 35% % who actually re- offended
COMPAS labels more Black defendants as "high risk" who do NOT re-offend (false positives: 45% for Black, 28% for white)
Black defendants are over-punished; they receive higher sentences for the same behavior
When COMPAS gives a high-risk score, that score predicts re-offending equally well for both groups ("calibrated")
Similarly, when it gives a low-risk score, that predicts non-re-offending equally well for both groups
The algorithm is equally accurate; the difference in false positive rates reflects different base rates of crime in the population
False positive rates equal across groups (same % of innocent people falsely labeled "high risk")
Same score = same likelihood of re-offending, regardless of race
COMPAS is equally accurate for both groups
The Deeper Problem: Base Rate Difference
When base rates (true re-offending rates) differ between groups, it is impossible to achieve equal false positive rates AND equal false negative rates simultaneously.

If Black defendants have a higher base rate of re-offending, a well-calibrated algorithm will necessarily label more of them "high risk" to correctly reflect that higher rate. But this means more Black defendants will be falsely labeled if the algorithm tries to keep false positive rates equal across groups.

This is not a bug in COMPAS—it is a fundamental trade-off. No algorithm can satisfy both equalized odds and calibration when base rates differ. Choosing which metric to optimize is choosing whose errors to accept: equal error rates for innocent people, or equal predictive accuracy for the algorithm?
Both ProPublica and Northpointe were correct by different fairness metrics. COMPAS fails equalized odds and passes calibration.

You cannot have it all. Choosing a metric means choosing whose errors you prioritize. This is not a technical question—it is a values question. Are you more concerned about false positives (protecting innocent people) or about equal accuracy (treating the algorithm's predictions equally)? There is no single answer.
Fails (45% vs 28%) False positive rates equal across groups
Passes Same risk score = same likelihood of re-offending, regardless of race
Fails (45% vs 28%) False positive rates equal across groups
Passes Same risk score = same likelihood of re-offending, regardless of race
Bias does not appear in the model alone. It enters at every stage: data collection, labeling, model design, deployment, and feedback loops.

Bias is a pipeline problem, not a model problem. Fixing the model alone (with clever algorithms or fairness constraints) will not work if the data is biased or if the deployment context is unfair.
Bias can be addressed before training (pre-processing), during training (in-processing), or after training (post-processing).
Reweight samples to balance groups; collect more data from underrepresented groups
Add fairness constraints (e.g., force equal false positive rates); adjust loss function to penalize unfair predictions
Adjust prediction thresholds per group; re-calibrate scores to equalize error rates

Fixing the training data addresses the root cause. In-processing is flexible but complex. Post-processing is easy but fragile—if you adjust thresholds, the model still has learned biased patterns and may fail on new data.
Practical Checklist: Five Questions Before Deployment
Before deploying a model, answer these five questions in order. If "no" or "I don't know," apply the recommended mitigation and reassess.
Collect more data or reweight Have you
for missing groups? 1 Pick one Have you
across groups? 3 Reweight, threshold adjust, or constrain Have you
? 4 Set up regular audits Will you
Collect more data or reweight Have you
for missing groups? 1 Pick one Have you
across groups? 3 Reweight, threshold adjust, or constrain Have you
? 4 Set up regular audits Will you
Have you audited your data for missing groups?
If no → Collect more data or reweight samples to balance groups
Have you chosen a fairness metric?
If no → Pick one (equalized odds? calibration? demographic parity?). Acknowledge you are making a value judgment.
Have you measured that metric across groups?
If no → Run the numbers. Break down performance by demographic group and compare.
Have you tried at least one mitigation?
If no → Apply pre, in, or post-processing intervention. Reassess metric.
If no → Set up regular audits. Fairness is not a one-time fix. New biases can emerge as users interact with the system.
Fairness is a process, not a product.

Bias enters at every stage (data → label → model → deploy → feedback). You must audit, choose metrics, mitigate, monitor, then repeat. A model that passes fairness tests today may fail when deployed, or fail on new data next year.
Training data over-represents one group (men) because they were historically hired more.
Reweight female resumes to have higher weight during training. The model "cares more" about getting female examples correct because it is penalized more heavily when it gets them wrong.
If a female resume has the same pattern as a male resume, the algorithm learns to treat them equivalently during training. Reweighting corrects for the imbalanced historical data.

Reweighting is not a magic wand. It does not fix the underlying historical bias in the true hiring outcomes (which were genuinely male-dominated). But it forces the model to learn patterns from female resumes equally well, which reduces the propagation of historical bias.

Reinforcement Learning & Fairness in Machine Learning
Source: Lecture 10 (Reinforcement Learning) & Lecture 11 (Bias, Fairness & Ethics in ML)
Topic: How agents learn opti/flashmal behavior through reward signals, and how to build ML systems that are fair across groups.
Reinforcement Learning: Core Concepts and Q-Learning
Bias in Machine Learning: Sources, Detection, and Mitigation
Reinforcement Learning: Core Concepts and Q-Learning
Overview
What: Building systems that learn optimal decision-making by interacting with an environment and receiving reward signals, without explicit instruction.
How it breaks down:
Foundations of Reinforcement Learning — the agent-environment model and the core components that make RL distinct from supervised/unsupervised learning
Value Functions and Q-Learning — how to represent the "goodness" of states and actions, and the algorithm that learns those values
The Q-Learning Update Process — the Bellman equation, temporal difference error, and how to iteratively refine Q-values through episodes
Convergence and Multiple Episodes — why one attempt is not enough and how repeated experience stabilizes learning
Takeaway: Q-Learning turns a sequence of observed rewards into a mental model (Q-table) that the agent can use to make optimal decisions in any state, and that model improves with every episode as long as the agent explores enough to discover all paths.
Foundations of Reinforcement Learning
The Three Branches of Machine Learning
Reinforcement Learning: Learning what to do (which action to take) based on rewards and punishments received from the environment.
Supervised Learning: Map input → output (student with answer key)
Unsupervised Learning: Find hidden patterns (explorer finding tribes)
Reinforcement Learning: Actions → maximize reward (pet learning tricks for treats)
RL differs fundamentally because there is no teacher providing the correct answer. The agent only receives feedback on how good or bad an action was, and must learn which actions lead to high rewards through trial and experience.
The Five Core Components
Components: The five elements that define every reinforcement learning problem.
Agent: The learner (e.g., the robot)
Environment: The world the agent interacts with (e.g., the grid)
Action: What the agent can do (e.g., move up/down/left/right)
State: Where the agent is at any moment (e.g., a specific cell in the grid)
Reward: Feedback signal from the environment (+ good, − bad, 0 neutral)
The "No Teacher" Principle
No Teacher Principle: The agent receives only feedback signals (rewards/penalties), not instructions or a map, and must gradually learn which actions lead to better outcomes through accumulation.
Exploration phase: Agent takes actions and receives feedback (warmer/colder → small ±reward; candy/lemon → large ±reward)
Learning mechanism: No correct path is given; agent improves by accumulating experience over time
Core insight: This separation of learning from instruction is what makes RL powerful: it works in environments where the "right" answer depends on context, opponent behavior, or unknown dynamics
Like a pet learning tricks for treats: there is no manual showing the pet the correct behavior. The pet tries actions, receives rewards or not, and gradually learns which actions reliably produce the treat.
When to Use Reinforcement Learning
RL Applications: Domains where no fixed "correct" answer exists, opponent behavior is adaptive, or the environment is unknown or changing.

The Exploration-Exploitation Dilemma: Should I do what I already know works (exploit), or try something new that might be better (explore)? RL agents must balance greedy choices (highest known Q-value) with random exploration (discovering better paths).
Value Functions and Q-Learning
Value Functions
Value Function: A function that estimates how good a state or state-action pair is, by predicting the total reward an agent will receive from that point onward.
State Value V(s): How good it is to be in a given state s (the expected future reward from that state)
State-Action Value Q(s,a): How good it is to take a specific action a in a given state s (the expected future reward after taking that action)
Q-Learning is a value-based method: it learns a value function that, when maximized over actions, determines the optimal policy.
The Q-Table: State-Action Value Matrix
Q-Table: A lookup table storing Q(s,a) for every state-action pair, where each entry represents the estimated long-term value of taking that action in that state.

Rows = States (S1, S2, S3, S4)
Columns = Actions (A1, A2, A3, A4)
Cell contents = Q(s,a), the value estimate for that pair
At the start of learning, Q-values are initialized arbitrarily (often to 0 or random numbers). The algorithm corrects them over time. Even if the initial guess is wrong, the learning process converges toward the true values as the agent gains experience.
The Q-Learning Update Process
The Bellman Equation
Bellman Equation: The observed Q-value is the immediate reward plus the discounted maximum future Q-value available from the next state.
Formula for observed Q-value

Q(s,a)_observed: The computed Q-value after this experience
R(s'): The immediate reward received upon arriving in the next state s'
γ (gamma): Discount factor; how much the agent values future rewards relative to immediate rewards
max_a' Q(s', a'): The best Q-value available from the next state (across all possible actions)
The Bellman equation decomposes value into two parts: what you get right now (immediate reward) plus what you can get next (future value, discounted). This recursive structure is why Q-Learning learns efficiently: each update leverages what the agent already knows about future states.
Discount Factor γ (Gamma)
Discount Factor γ: A number between 0 and 1 that controls how much the agent cares about future rewards compared to immediate rewards.
γ = 0: Robot only cares about immediate reward. The future does not matter; only the next step counts.
γ = 0.5: Future rewards matter half as much as immediate rewards.
γ = 0.9: Future rewards matter significantly, but slightly less than today's rewards.
γ = 1: Robot values future rewards equally to immediate rewards (all time steps equally important).
A higher γ makes the agent more tolerant of short-term negative rewards when future rewards are promising. This is crucial in environments where the path to the goal incurs temporary costs (like moving through a low-reward zone to reach a high-reward target).
Temporal Difference Error (TDE)
Temporal Difference Error: The difference between the observed Q-value (what the agent just learned from experience) and the expected Q-value (what the agent previously thought).
Temporal Difference Error

Observed: The Q-value computed from the Bellman equation after one action and reward
Expected: The Q-value stored in the table before this experience
TDE measures how "surprised" the agent was by this experience. A large positive TDE means the path was better than expected; a large negative TDE means it was worse. This error signal drives learning.
The Q-Value Update Rule
Update Rule: Adjust the stored Q-value toward the observed Q-value, scaled by the learning rate.
Q-value update rule

α (alpha): Learning rate; how much to adjust the Q-value at each time step (typically 0 < α ≤ 1)
TDE: Temporal difference error (observed − expected)
Small α (e.g., 0.1): Conservative updates; changes are gradual, reducing noise but learning is slower
Large α (e.g., 0.9): Aggressive updates; the new observation heavily overrides the old value, but may oscillate
The update rule is not a replacement—it is a weighted blend of the old Q-value and the new observation. This averaging across experiences is why Q-values eventually stabilize rather than jumping erratically.
Worked Example: S1 → S4

Convergence and Multiple Episodes
What is an Episode
Episode: One complete run from start to goal (or failure), during which the agent takes actions and receives rewards until a terminal state is reached.
Start: Agent begins at a starting state (e.g., S1, or randomly chosen)
End: Agent reaches a goal state (e.g., S9 with +10 reward) or a failure state (e.g., S8 with −10 penalty)
Path example: S1 → down → S4 → right → S5 → right → S6 → ... (episode continues until goal or failure)
An episode is bounded. In a real task, "bounded" means the agent either reaches the goal or uses up its allotted steps. This is important: without an end condition, the agent would accumulate infinite rewards and learning would never stabilize.
Why One Episode Is Not Enough
Single-Episode Problem: After one episode, Q-values are unstable and inaccurate because the agent has not yet discovered all paths or experienced the full range of rewards.
The agent has only seen one path through the environment
It has not yet discovered the optimal route to the goal
It has not experienced high-reward outcomes (like +10)
Q-values reflect only the partial rewards seen so far (e.g., small negative rewards like −1, −2, −1)
These Q-values do not represent the true value of each state because they are missing critical information about what lies beyond
Convergence Fact: Q-values do not converge to optimal values after one episode. Multiple episodes with exploration are required because each episode provides only a partial sample of the environment's reward structure.
Why Multiple Episodes Are Needed
Multiple Episodes: Each episode gives the agent more experience, allowing it to discover better paths, update Q-values closer to the truth, and eventually converge on an optimal policy.
Exploration benefit: Different episodes may take different random actions, exploring new paths that lead to higher-reward states
Bootstrapping: When the agent reaches S5 in a later episode, its Q(S5, a) values are now more accurate (from previous episodes), so the Bellman update at earlier states backpropagates better value estimates
Convergence signal: When Q-values stop changing much between episodes, the agent has learned the environment's reward structure and the policy has stabilized
Optimal policy: Once Q-values have converged, the agent can extract the optimal policy by always choosing the action with the highest Q-value in each state
Learning cycle: Audit (run episode) → Update (refine Q-values) → Explore (try new actions) → Repeat. Each cycle brings Q-values closer to the true value, which represents the discounted future reward from each state-action pair.
Bias in Machine Learning: Sources, Detection, and Mitigation
Overview
What: Understanding how human biases enter ML systems, how they cause unfair outcomes across groups, how to measure and detect bias, and what interventions work.
How it breaks down:
Why Fairness Matters — the business, quality, and ethical imperatives for building fair systems
The Four Types of Bias — where bias enters the pipeline (historical, representation, measurement, aggregation) and how to recognize each
Real-World Case Studies — Amazon hiring (historical), Optum healthcare (measurement), Gender Shades facial recognition (representation), COMPAS recidivism (fairness metrics in conflict)
Detection and Mitigation — a practical framework: audit data, choose fairness metrics, measure performance by group, apply interventions (pre/in/post-processing), and monitor after deployment
Takeaway: Bias is not a property of the algorithm alone—it is a property of the entire pipeline (data, labels, model, deployment, feedback). Every model must be audited across groups, and no single fairness metric can satisfy all stakeholders; the choice of metric embeds a value judgment about whose errors to prioritize.
Why Fairness Matters
ML Is Not Neutral
Non-Neutrality: ML models are trained on human-generated data, which encodes human decisions and human biases. Models do not correct or erase these biases; they amplify, automate, and legitimize them.
Past human decisions → Training data (encoded with bias)
Model learns patterns from that data → Learns to replicate and generalize bias
Model deployed → Biased decisions applied at scale, automatically, and with the appearance of objectivity
The appearance of mathematical objectivity makes algorithmic bias more dangerous than human bias. A human hiring manager might catch themselves and correct a prejudiced decision. An algorithm looks like math and is trusted without question.
Real-World Impact: High-Stakes Domains
High-Stakes Impact: Biased ML systems have caused measurable harm to real people across employment, healthcare, and criminal justice.

Jobs: Resume screeners filter out candidates based on gender or race, blocking opportunities
Healthcare: Algorithms undertreating minority patients because they use proxy measures that reflect access barriers, not true health need
Justice: Risk assessment tools overpredict recidivism for certain demographic groups, leading to harsher sentences and parole denials
Three reasons to care: (1) Business risk — lawsuits, audits, brand damage; (2) Model quality — bias = poor generalization to new groups; (3) Ethics — you have power; power creates responsibility.
What Is Bias in ML?
Algorithmic Bias: Systematic, unfair discrimination in model outputs that creates different outcomes for different groups, where group membership should not matter.
Bias vs. Other Differences

Not all differences are bias. Bias = difference + unjustified + harmful. If a medical model predicts higher disease risk in a group that genuinely has higher prevalence (due to genetic or environmental factors), that is not bias—it is accuracy. Bias is when the difference reflects data quality, missing information, or historical injustice, not underlying reality.
The Four Types of Bias
Historical Bias
Historical Bias: Past social inequalities are reflected in training data, and the model learns to replicate them.
Core mechanism: The world is unfair. Data remembers that unfairness. The model learns from the data.
Example: A loan model trained on past lending approvals learns that certain zip codes (historically redlined by discriminatory policy) have higher default rates. Even if current residents are equally creditworthy, the model downgrades them because the historical data shows a pattern.
Historical bias is the hardest to fix because the bias is in the ground truth itself—the labels in the training data encode real-world discrimination. The model is not doing anything "wrong"; it is learning from biased history.
Representation Bias
Representation Bias: Training data does not reflect the real-world population; missing voices create blind spots.
Core mechanism: If you train only on data from one group, the model learns that group well and performs poorly on all others.
Example: A medical image AI trained mostly on fair-skinned patients performs poorly on darker skin tones. The algorithm never saw many examples of darker skin, so it has not learned the visual patterns that distinguish healthy skin from diseased skin in that population.
Representation bias is the most straightforward to identify: look at the demographics of your training data. If a group is underrepresented, the model will likely underperform on that group.
Measurement Bias
Measurement Bias: Features or labels are systematically different across groups, so the model learns the wrong thing.
Core mechanism: Using the wrong variable as a proxy for what you actually want to measure.
Example: Using past healthcare costs as a proxy for "health need." But lower-income or underserved groups have lower recorded costs not because they are healthier, but because they have less access to healthcare. The model learns: low costs = low need, and systematically excludes the sickest patients in those groups from extra care.
Similar to using zip code as a proxy for creditworthiness. Zip code is correlated with wealth and credit access due to historical segregation, but it does not measure a person's actual ability to repay. The model conflates geography with financial merit.
Aggregation Bias
Aggregation Bias: A single model forced onto groups with different base rates fails for both.
Core mechanism: One-size-fits-all does not work when the underlying populations have different characteristics.
Example: A single recidivism model for two neighborhoods with different crime rates and policing intensity. The model may appear "accurate" when averaged across both neighborhoods but is systematically wrong in each one individually because it cannot account for neighborhood-specific factors.
The fix for aggregation bias is often to build separate models for different groups or to include group-specific features. However, this must be done carefully: disaggregating can reduce data per group and increase variance, or it can be justified as accommodating real differences.
Quick Reference: Recognizing Bias Types
Case Study: Amazon Hiring
Context and Goal
Problem: Amazon needed to screen millions of resumes for thousands of hires per year. Manual screening was slow and inconsistent.
Amazon's intuition: If ML can recommend products, why can't it recommend resumes?
The plan: Train on past resumes and hiring decisions, let the algorithm learn which resumes led to hires, then rank new resumes automatically
Expected benefits: Faster, scalable, consistent
What Went Wrong
The Problem: The model learned from old resumes submitted by people already hired. Most of those people were men. The model learned to prefer men.
Biased training signal: Past hiring decisions reflected a male-dominated tech industry
Model's learned rules (discovered by analysis): Penalize the word "women," downgrade graduates from all-women's colleges, assign lower scores to female-sounding activities
Model's logic (without malice): "Most successful past hires were men" → "Resumes like those (male) → higher probability of hire" → "I should rank resumes of men higher"
Outcome: A woman applying to Amazon would have her resume downranked not because of anything she wrote, but because of patterns in the male-dominated hiring history
The model learned a correlation (male ≈ hired) but inverted causality (hiring is not male because males are better; males were hired because of historical discrimination). The model repeated that mistake.
What Happened After: The Fix Attempts
Timeline: Bias discovered (2015) → tool discontinued (2017), but attempts to fix failed in between.
2014: Amazon starts building the tool
2015: Internal team discovers gender bias
2017: Amazon discontinues the tool entirely
Why the fix failed: Engineers tried to remove gender-related words from the model, adjusted thresholds, ran new tests. But the bias kept coming back through hidden correlations.
If you remove the word "women," the model might learn to penalize typical women's colleges or female-coded activities by name
If you remove those, it might learn to penalize gap years (more common in female resumes in some fields)
The underlying problem—that the training data contains a male-dominated history—cannot be patched by removing features. You must fix the data.
Bias Type Identification: Amazon hiring is a Historical Bias case. The model learned from data that encoded past discrimination. Removing features is post-hoc and fragile. The real solution would have been to reweight training data to balance gender, or audit and correct the hiring decisions in the historical data itself.
Case Study: Optum Healthcare Algorithm
Context and Goal
Problem: Optum built an algorithm to identify "high-risk" patients who need extra care (nurses, check-ins, follow-ups).
Logic: Predict future healthcare costs → higher predicted cost = "high risk" → send extra resources
Assumption: Healthcare costs reflect health need
The Proxy Problem
The Proxy Problem: Using past healthcare costs as a proxy for "how sick is this patient?" breaks down when groups have different access to care.

For white patients (higher access): Recorded costs ≈ actual health need. Someone with a chronic illness gets diagnosed and treated, costs are recorded accurately.
For Black patients (lower access): Recorded costs << actual health need. Someone with the same chronic illness might not have regular access to doctors, so only emergencies are recorded. Costs look low even though the need is high.
The algorithm systematically excluded the sickest patients in the lowest-access group. At the same level of illness severity, Black patients were half as likely to be flagged for extra care.
The Fix
Timeline: Investigation began (2017) → published in Science (2019) → Optum modified algorithm (2019).
Original label: Past healthcare costs
New label: Number of chronic conditions + adjustment for access barriers
Why it works: "Number of chronic conditions" is more directly a measure of health need and is less mediated by access to the healthcare system
Bias Type Identification: Optum is a Measurement Bias case. The label (past costs) did not validly measure the target (health need) across groups. The fix was to choose a better label, not to remove groups or adjust thresholds.
Case Study: Gender Shades Facial Recognition
The Personal Discovery
Incident (2015): Joy Buolamwini, an MIT grad student, was working on a facial recognition project for a class. The software worked perfectly on her light-skinned classmates and even recognized a white beauty mask she held up. When she looked at the camera: no detection.
The model was literally blind to her face. This motivated a research question: Is this algorithm trained only on light-skinned faces?
The Hypothesis and Experiment
Hypothesis: Facial recognition algorithms trained on datasets that are mostly light-skinned faces will perform well on that group and poorly on darker-skinned faces.
What Joy and her team did:
Analyzed existing facial recognition datasets (IJB-A, Adience)
Found representation bias: 80-86% light-skinned faces, only 14-20% darker-skinned faces
Created a balanced test dataset: 1,270 faces, equal representation from 3 African countries + 3 European countries, balanced by gender and skin type
Tested 3 commercial systems: IBM, Microsoft, Face++
The Results: Intersectional Failures
Finding: Error rates were highest for darker-skinned females—a phenomenon called intersectionality (multiple marginalized categories compound).

Best performance (0.3% error): Lighter-skinned males
Moderate (7-12% error): Lighter-skinned females and darker-skinned males
Worst performance (up to 34.7% error): Darker-skinned females
Company breakdown:
Microsoft: Over 93% of misgendered faces were darker-skinned subjects
Face++: Over 95% of misgendered faces were female
IBM: Largest gap (34.4% difference between best and worst groups)
Intersectionality Insight: Bias does not affect demographic groups independently. A woman of color can face compounded bias (both gender and race). Gender Shades showed that the three systems failed darkest on the intersection of female + darker-skinned, not just on skin tone or gender alone.
Industry Response and Improvement
Impact: The Gender Shades study changed how companies audit facial recognition systems.
Immediate (2018): IBM responded in one day, announced changes to Watson Visual Recognition. Microsoft and Face++ began audits and retraining.
One year later (2019 follow-up audit):
Microsoft: 19.28% error reduction for darker females
IBM: 17.73% error reduction
Face++: 30.4% error reduction (biggest improvement)
Improvements were significant but error rates remained higher for darker-skinned subjects. This shows both that the problem is fixable (data + retraining helps) and persistent (structural bias in datasets and development practices is slow to change).
Bias Type Identification: Gender Shades is a Representation Bias case. Training data was 80-86% light-skinned faces. The model was never exposed to enough darker-skinned examples to learn those patterns well. The fix: collect more diverse data and retrain.
Case Study: COMPAS Recidivism Prediction
Context and Use
COMPAS: An algorithm used in over 1 million cases across US courts to predict whether a defendant will re-offend within 2 years.
Developer: Northpointe
Use in court: Judges receive a risk score (1-10) for each defendant; scores influence bail amounts, sentencing, and parole decisions
Prediction target: Recidivism (whether someone will be re-arrested within 2 years)
The ProPublica Investigation
Question: Is COMPAS fair? Do risk scores mean the same thing across racial groups?
Methodology:
Obtained COMPAS scores for 7,000+ defendants in Broward County, Florida (2013-2014)
Tracked whether they actually re-offended within 2 years
Compared model performance across white and Black defendants
Key Finding: COMPAS showed different error patterns across groups.
The Fairness Conflict: Two Metrics, Two Narratives
The Dilemma: ProPublica and Northpointe both measured fairness, got opposite conclusions, and were both technically correct.



ProPublica's claim (False Positive Rate):
COMPAS labels more Black defendants as "high risk" who do NOT re-offend (false positives: 45% for Black, 28% for white)
Interpretation: Black defendants are over-punished; they receive higher sentences for the same behavior
Northpointe's defense (Calibration):
When COMPAS gives a high-risk score, that score predicts re-offending equally well for both groups ("calibrated")
Similarly, when it gives a low-risk score, that predicts non-re-offending equally well for both groups
Interpretation: The algorithm is equally accurate; the difference in false positive rates reflects different base rates of crime in the population
Fairness Metric Conflict

The Deeper Problem: Base Rate Difference
Mathematical Impossibility: When base rates (true re-offending rates) differ between groups, it is impossible to achieve equal false positive rates AND equal false negative rates simultaneously.
White defendants: ~35% actually re-offend
Black defendants: ~52% actually re-offend
Why this matters: If Black defendants have a higher base rate of re-offending, a well-calibrated algorithm will necessarily label more of them "high risk" to correctly reflect that higher rate. But this means more Black defendants will be falsely labeled if the algorithm tries to keep false positive rates equal across groups.
This is not a bug in COMPAS—it is a fundamental trade-off. No algorithm can satisfy both equalized odds and calibration when base rates differ. Choosing which metric to optimize is choosing whose errors to accept: equal error rates for innocent people, or equal predictive accuracy for the algorithm?
The Fairness Question
Key Insight: Both ProPublica and Northpointe were correct by different fairness metrics. COMPAS fails equalized odds and passes calibration.
Different fairness metrics can conflict. You cannot have it all. Choosing a metric means choosing whose errors you prioritize. This is not a technical question—it is a values question. Are you more concerned about false positives (protecting innocent people) or about equal accuracy (treating the algorithm's predictions equally)? There is no single answer.



Detection and Mitigation Framework
The Bias Pipeline
Core Insight: Bias does not appear in the model alone. It enters at every stage: data collection, labeling, model design, deployment, and feedback loops.

Bias is a pipeline problem, not a model problem. Fixing the model alone (with clever algorithms or fairness constraints) will not work if the data is biased or if the deployment context is unfair.
Three Intervention Points
Interventions: Bias can be addressed before training (pre-processing), during training (in-processing), or after training (post-processing).

Pre-processing is the most robust. Fixing the training data addresses the root cause. In-processing is flexible but complex. Post-processing is easy but fragile—if you adjust thresholds, the model still has learned biased patterns and may fail on new data.
Practical Checklist: Five Questions Before Deployment
Audit Framework: Before deploying a model, answer these five questions in order. If "no" or "I don't know," apply the recommended mitigation and reassess.

Have you audited your data for missing groups?
If no → Collect more data or reweight samples to balance groups
Have you chosen a fairness metric?
If no → Pick one (equalized odds? calibration? demographic parity?). Acknowledge you are making a value judgment.
Have you measured that metric across groups?
If no → Run the numbers. Break down performance by demographic group and compare.
Have you tried at least one mitigation?
If no → Apply pre, in, or post-processing intervention. Reassess metric.
Will you monitor after deployment?
If no → Set up regular audits. Fairness is not a one-time fix. New biases can emerge as users interact with the system.
Fairness is a process, not a product. Bias enters at every stage (data → label → model → deploy → feedback). You must audit, choose metrics, mitigate, monitor, then repeat. A model that passes fairness tests today may fail when deployed, or fail on new data next year.
Pre-processing Example: Reweighting (Amazon Case)
Problem: Training data over-represents one group (men) because they were historically hired more.
Solution: Reweight female resumes to have higher weight during training. The model "cares more" about getting female examples correct because it is penalized more heavily when it gets them wrong.
Effect: If a female resume has the same pattern as a male resume, the algorithm learns to treat them equivalently during training. Reweighting corrects for the imbalanced historical data.
Reweighting is not a magic wand. It does not fix the underlying historical bias in the true hiring outcomes (which were genuinely male-dominated). But it forces the model to learn patterns from female resumes equally well, which reduces the propagation of historical bias.
